title: Adult relationship quality is associated with childhood family belonging, health, financial security, and adversity across countries, but the strength of pathways varies by context
source_unit: Wilkinson et al., Life course insights into social relationship quality: a cross-national analysis of 22 countries, Scientific Reports 2025
geography: 22 countries in Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study, including the United States, United Kingdom, and diverse non-Western contexts

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; childhood conditions and adult relationship quality

denominator.unit: adults in nationally representative samples across 22 countries

parent_relationships.value: better reported relationships with mother and father during childhood were associated with higher adult social relationship quality

childhood_abuse.value: experiencing abuse during childhood was associated with lower adult social relationship quality

family_outsider.value: feeling like an outsider in one’s family while growing up was associated with lower adult social relationship quality

life_course_route.value: early family belonging and adversity may accumulate into later relational advantage or disadvantage

observations.method: Country-specific multivariate regression and random-effects meta-analysis using nationally representative Wave 1 Global Flourishing Study samples; childhood factors were retrospectively reported in adulthood.
observations.uncertainty: The design is cross-sectional and retrospective, so associations are not longitudinal causal estimates; recall bias, unmeasured confounding, relationship-quality effects on recall, and cross-cultural interpretation remain possible.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 22 countries, analyzed by childhood family relationships, abuse, family belonging, health, financial status, religious attendance, age cohort, and sociodemographic characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adult relationship quality may shape how people remember childhood, and common causes such as mental health, family resources, neighborhood conditions, or later institutional experiences may explain part of the association.

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; childhood health and financial security

childhood_health.value: excellent or very good self-rated childhood health was associated with higher adult relationship quality, while fair childhood health was associated with lower quality relative to good health

subjective_financial_status.value: higher subjective financial status during childhood was associated with higher adult relationship quality

resource_route.value: health and economic resources may enable time, mobility, confidence, and shared activities that support later relationships

inequality_route.value: relational outcomes can carry forward childhood inequalities even when adult relationship quality is measured subjectively

observations.method: Multivariate country-specific models and pooled random-effects meta-analysis of retrospective childhood health and financial-status measures.
observations.uncertainty: Childhood health and financial status are self-reported retrospectively; socioeconomic position, adult health, family structure, and national welfare context may confound associations, and the study does not identify a specific intervention pathway.
observations.subgroup: Adults with different childhood health and subjective financial circumstances across 22 countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with stronger adult relationships may recall childhood conditions more positively; material resources may proxy parental care, education, neighborhood safety, or later opportunity rather than directly producing relationship quality.

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; cross-national heterogeneity of childhood pathways

abuse_heterogeneity.value: the association between childhood abuse and adult relationship quality was largest in Poland and smallest in Sweden, with limited evidence in Germany, Hong Kong, and India

parent_pathways.value: parent relationship associations differed by country: some showed maternal effects, some paternal effects, some both, and some neither

family_structure.value: associations for parental divorce or parental death differed in direction across countries

contextual_mechanism.value: national norms, gender roles, family systems, welfare conditions, and cultural meanings may shape how childhood experiences carry into adult relationships

observations.method: Country-specific analyses alongside random-effects meta-analysis, with heterogeneity statistics and sensitivity analyses reported by the authors.
observations.uncertainty: The exploratory design does not identify why country coefficients differ; differences may reflect measurement, translation, sampling, reporting, institutional context, or true social mechanisms.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 22 national contexts, with childhood experiences and family structures interpreted within country-specific social systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-country coefficient differences should not be read as national rankings of family quality or resilience; observed heterogeneity may reflect survey comparability limits.

denominator.unit: cross-national exploratory life-course study and its proposed research agenda

early_intervention_route.value: protective childhood relationships, prevention of abuse, family belonging, health, and material security are identified as upstream conditions for later relational well-being

social_infrastructure_route.value: family, schools, health systems, religious communities, neighborhoods, and economic supports may shape relational capacity over the life course

measurement_boundary.value: the study calls for deeper research by relationship type and more direct examination of mechanisms rather than treating global relationship quality as a single endpoint

cumulative_exposure.value: relational well-being should be read as accumulated across childhood, health, economic resources, family belonging, and later social institutions

observations.method: Authors' synthesis of exploratory cross-national associations and stated future research implications.
observations.uncertainty: The paper does not evaluate interventions or prove that changing any upstream factor will improve adult relationship quality; policy implications require longitudinal and quasi-experimental testing.
observations.subgroup: Children, families, schools, health and social-service systems, communities, and adults experiencing early-life advantage or adversity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early-life interventions may improve many outcomes without producing the same relational effects across cultures; formal systems can support relationships but can also impose stigma or surveillance.

related_sources.claim: Open-access Scientific Reports article using Global Flourishing Study data from 202,898 adults in 22 countries to examine childhood antecedents of adult relationship quality.
Publisher PDF for the 2025 peer-reviewed article.

boundary: This record adds a life-course mechanism from childhood family relationships, abuse, belonging, health, and financial security through adult relationship quality and cross-national heterogeneity. It is exploratory retrospective cross-sectional evidence, not longitudinal causal proof, an intervention evaluation, or a claim that national culture alone determines adult relationships.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Publisher article reviewed for sample, childhood predictors, adult relationship-quality measure, pooled associations, country-specific heterogeneity, policy-relevant pathways, and limitations including recall and causal boundaries.
